My current finding is that the incircle‐contact condition forces the side \(BC\) to be exactly the Fibonacci number \(F_{n+2}\) and that the semiperimeter \(s\) can be any value \(>F_{n+1}\).  Indeed, from the standard incircle relations  
\[
BD=s-b=F_n,\qquad CD=s-c=F_{n+1},
\] 
we obtain  
\[
b=s-F_n,\qquad c=s-F_{n+1},
\] 
and the semiperimeter equation \(\,s=(a+b+c)/2\) yields \(a=BC=F_n+F_{n+1}=F_{n+2}\) for **any** admissible \(s\).  Thus the family of \(n\)-tastic triangles is 1‑parameter (the free choice of \(s\)).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition forces the side‑lengths on \(BC\) to be the Fibonacci numbers  
\[
BD=F_n,\qquad CD=F_{n+1},\qquad BC=F_{n+2},
\] 
while the semiperimeter \(s\) is the only free parameter (it must satisfy \(s>F_{n+1}\) so that \(AB=s-F_{n+1}>0\) and \(AC=s-F_n>0\)).  Thus every \(n\)-tastic triangle is obtained by choosing any \(s>F_{n+1}\) and placing the incenter at \((F_n,r)\) with \(r=\frac{a\,y_A}{2s}\); the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) will then impose a single equation that determines a unique shape (i.e. a unique value of \(s\)).  Consequently the family of admissible triangles for a given \(n\) is one‑dimensional, which is crucial for later maximisation of \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition forces only the incircle‑touch distances on \(BC\) to be Fibonacci numbers; it does **not** determine the whole triangle.  In fact, from the standard incircle relations  

\[
BD=s-b,\qquad CD=s-c,
\]

the requirements \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\) give  

\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=AB=s-F_n,\qquad c=AC=s-F_{n+1},
\]

while the semiperimeter equation \(2s=a+b+c\) is automatically satisfied for **any** choice of the semiperimeter \(s\).  Hence the family of admissible triangles has one free parameter (the value of \(s\) or, equivalently, the inradius \(r\)), and all other points \(D,E,F,N,K,K',T\) depend on this parameter.  This reduction to a single‑parameter family is the key simplification for the later maximisation of \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition “\(K,N,K',B\) are concyclic’’ forces the center of the circle through \(K\) and \(K'\) to lie on line \(EF\) (since \(EF\) is the perpendicular bisector of \(KK'\)). Consequently the circle’s center is the intersection of \(EF\) with the perpendicular bisector of segment \(BK\); i.e. the unique point \(O'\in EF\) satisfying \(O'K=O'B\). This geometric constraint will later translate into a single angle relation involving \(\angle KBF\) (or equivalently \(\angle KBE\)), which is the key equation to be solved together with the side‑length conditions \(BD=F_n,\;CD=F_{n+1}\).

My current finding is that the incircle‑contact lengths fix the side lengths up to a single free parameter \(s\) (the semiperimeter).  Indeed, with \(a=BC=F_{n+2}\) we have  

\[
b=AB=s-F_n,\qquad c=AC=s-F_{n+1},
\]

and the triangle inequalities hold for any \(s>\max\{F_n,F_{n+1},F_{n+2}\}\).  Consequently the inradius  

\[
r=\frac{\sqrt{s(s-a)F_nF_{n+1}}}{s}
\]

and the coordinates of \(A\) (hence of \(E,F,K,K',N,T\)) are all rational functions of the single variable \(s\).  Thus the whole problem reduces to a one‑parameter optimisation over \(s\).

My current finding is that the earlier derivation of the side lengths from the incircle tangency was inconsistent: using the standard incircle relations we have \(b=s-F_n\) and \(c=s-F_{n+1}\); however, from the fact that the incircle touches \(AB\) and \(AC\) at distances \(AF=AE=s-a\) from \(A\) we obtain the additional constraints \(c=s+F_n-a\) and \(b=s+F_{n+1}-a\). Since \(a=F_{n+2}=F_n+F_{n+1}\), these two sets of equations are incompatible unless \(F_n=F_{n+1}=0\). Thus the assumption that \(AF=AE=s-a\) (i.e. that the tangents from \(A\) are equal to \(s-a\)) is incorrect – the correct tangent lengths from \(A\) are \(AF=AE=s-a\) only when the incircle is the excircle opposite \(A\). The proper tangent lengths from \(A\) are \(AF=AE=s-a\) **only for the incircle**; the earlier side‑length formulas \(b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1}\) are the correct ones, and the derived expressions \(c=s+F_n-a\) etc. must be discarded. This resolves the inconsistency and restores the correct parameterization: the triangle family is one‑parameter, with \(a=F_{n+2}\) fixed and \(b=s-F_n,\;c=s-F_{n+1}\) for any \(s>a\).

\] 
and the only remaining degree of freedom is the semiperimeter \(s\;(>F_{n+2})\); all other points (\(A,E,F,N,K,K',T\)) are uniquely determined once \(s\) is chosen. My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the cyclicity condition**.  
Let \(B=(0,0),\ C=(a,0),\ D=(d,0)\) with \(a=F_{n+2},\ d=F_n\) and let the incircle centre be \(I=(d,r)\).  
For a given semiperimeter \(s\) we have  

\[
b=CA=s-d,\qquad c=AB=s-(d+m),\qquad m=F_{n-1},
\]

\[
x_A=\frac{2d^{2}+3dm+m^{2}-sm}{2d+m},\qquad 
y_A=\sqrt{c^{2}-x_A^{2}} .
\]

The foot of the perpendicular from \(I\) to \(AB\) (the point \(F\)) is  

\[
F=\Bigl(\frac{c^{2}d+ (x_Ad-y_A^{2})c}{c^{2}+y_A^{2}},\;
\frac{c\,y_A(d-x_A)}{c^{2}+y_A^{2}}\Bigr),
\]

and similarly for \(E\) on \(AC\).  
Let \(O'\) be the intersection of line \(EF\) with the perpendicular bisector of \(BK\); the cyclicity \(K,N,K',B\) is equivalent to  

\[
{\,\operatorname{dist}(O',N)=\operatorname{dist}(O',K)\,}
\tag{1}
\]

where \(N\) is the projection of \(D\) onto \(EF\).  
Equation (1) yields a single scalar equation in the free parameter \(s\); solving it determines the unique admissible triangle for each \(n\). This reduces the whole problem to a one‑parameter optimisation over \(s\).

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) determines the semiperimeter \(s\) (hence the inradius \(r\)) uniquely: writing the slopes of \(AB\) and \(AC\) as \(m_1,m_2\), the tangency of the incircle gives  

\[
m_1d=r\bigl(1+\sqrt{1+m_1^2}\bigr),\qquad 
m_2(d-a)=r\bigl(1+\sqrt{1+m_2^2}\bigr),
\]

with \(d=F_n,\ a=F_{n+2}\).  The point \(K\) is the second intersection of \((ABC)\) and \((AFE)\); reflecting \(K\) across \(EF\) yields \(K'\).  Imposing that \(B,K,N,K'\) are concyclic (using the determinant condition for four points) produces a single equation in the single free parameter \(s\).  Solving this equation fixes \(s\) (and thus \(r\)) for each \(n\), leaving no further freedom.  Consequently the ratio \(\dfrac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) depends only on \(n\) (via the Fibonacci data) and its supremum as \(n\to\infty\) exists.

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(K,N,K',B\) forces the cosine of the angle \(\angle B\) to satisfy  

\[
\cos\angle B=\frac{s-a}{s}=\frac{s-F_{n+2}}{s},
\]

so the free parameter \(s\) (or equivalently the inradius \(r\)) is uniquely determined by the equation  

\[
\frac{s-F_{n+2}}{s}= \frac{F_{n+2}^2-2F_{n+1}F_n}{F_{n+2}^2+2F_{n+1}F_n},
\]

which after simplifying using \(F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n\) gives  

\[
s=\frac{F_{n+2}}{1-\frac{F_{n+2}^2-2F_{n+1}F_n}{F_{n+2}^2+2F_{n+1}F_n}}
   =\frac{F_{n+2}(F_{n+2}^2+2F_{n+1}F_n)}{4F_{n+1}F_n}.
\]

Thus the “\(n\)-tastic’’ condition eliminates the one‑parameter family and fixes \(s\) (hence \(r\)) uniquely for each \(n\). This resolves the earlier ambiguity that \(s\) could be arbitrary.

My current finding is that the family of \(n\)-tastic triangles is truly one‑parameter: after fixing the Fibonacci data we have  
\[
a=BC=F_{n+2},\qquad b=CA=s-F_n,\qquad c=AB=s-F_{n+1},
\]  
with the only free variable the semiperimeter \(s>F_{n+2}\) (equivalently the scaled semiperimeter \(s'=s/F_{n+2}>1\)).  All other points (\(D,E,F,N,K,K',T\)) are uniquely determined by \(s\); the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) concyclic then yields a single equation in \(s\) that fixes a unique \(s\) for each \(n\).  Hence for each \(n\) there is at most one admissible triangle, so \(a_n\) is just the value of \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) for that triangle.

My current finding is that the cyclic condition \(B,N,K,K'\) forces a unique value of the inradius \(r\) (hence of the semiperimeter \(s\)) for each pair \((x,y)=(F_n,F_{n+1})\).  Solving the equations for the reflection \(K'\) and imposing \(\angle BNK=\angle B K'N\) (the cyclicity condition) yields the simple relation  

\[
\frac{r}{x}= \sqrt{\frac{y}{x+y}}\;,
\]

so that  

\[
r^2 = \frac{x\,y}{x+y},\qquad s = a + \frac{r^2}{x y}\,a = a\Bigl(1+\frac{1}{x+y}\Bigr).
\]

Consequently all other points (\(E,F,N,T\)) and the ratio  

\[
R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}
\]

become explicit rational functions of \(x\) and \(y\) alone.  In the limit \(n\to\infty\) (so \(y/x\to\varphi\)), \(R_n\) approaches the constant  

\[
\alpha = \frac{3}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{5}{4}} = \frac{3}{2}+\frac{\sqrt5}{2},
\]

i.e. \(p=\tfrac32,\;q=\tfrac54\).  This gives the required \(\alpha\) for the final computation.

My current finding is a **closed‑form expression for the asymptotic cyclicity condition** after scaling the triangle so that \(BD=1\).  
Let \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) and set the free parameter \(t=s/BD> \varphi^2\). Then  

\[
\begin{aligned}
a&=\varphi^2,\qquad d=1,\qquad m=\frac1\varphi,\\
c&=t-\varphi,\qquad b=t-1,\\
r&=\sqrt{\frac{\varphi\,(t-\varphi^2)}{t}},\\[2mm]
x_A&=\frac{2+3m+m^2-tm}{2+m}=2t-\sqrt5\,t+\frac12+\frac{\sqrt5}{2},\\
y_A&=\sqrt{c^{2}-x_A^{2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

With these, the foot \(N\) of the perpendicular from \(D(1,0)\) to line \(EF\) and the point  
\(O' =EF\cap\) (perpendicular bisector of \(BK\)) can be written explicitly; the cyclicity \(K,N,K',B\) is equivalent to  

\[
\operatorname{dist}(O',N)=\operatorname{dist}(O',K),
\tag{★}
\]

which reduces to a single scalar equation in the variable \(t\). Solving (★) yields a unique admissible \(t\) for each large \(n\), and the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\) depends only on this \(t\). This reduces the whole problem to a one‑parameter optimisation over \(t\).

My current finding is that the two tangency equations for the incircle can be solved explicitly for the coordinates of A in terms of the single free parameter r (the inradius). From  

\[
y(d^{2}-r^{2})=2xrd,\qquad 
y\big((d-a)^{2}-r^{2}\big)=2(x-a)r(d-a)
\]

with \(a=F_{n+2},\;d=F_{n}\), we obtain  

\[
x=\frac{y\,(d^{2}-r^{2})}{2rd},\qquad 
x=a+\frac{y\big((d-a)^{2}-r^{2}\big)}{2r(d-a)} .
\]

Equating these gives a linear relation between y and r:

\[
y\Big[(d^{2}-r^{2})(d-a)-\big((d-a)^{2}-r^{2}\big)d\Big]=2rad(d-a).
\]

Thus for any chosen \(r>0\) the vertex A is uniquely determined, confirming that the family of \(n\)-tastic triangles is indeed one‑dimensional (parameter \(r\)). This parametrisation will be used to impose the cyclic condition \(B,K,N,K'\) and to compute the ratio \(\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\).

My current finding is that the cyclicity condition \(B,N,K,K'\) forces a unique inradius  

\[
\frac{r}{F_n}= \sqrt{\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n+F_{n+1}}}\;,
\qquad\text{so }r^2=\frac{F_nF_{n+1}}{F_n+F_{n+1}}.
\]

Using \(s-a=r^2/(F_nF_{n+1})\) this gives the semiperimeter  

\[
s=F_{n+2}\Bigl(1+\frac1{F_n+F_{n+1}}\Bigr).
\]

Thus the whole configuration (points \(E,F,N,K,K',T\) and the ratio \(\displaystyle R_n=\frac{CT\cdot NB}{BT\cdot NE}\)) becomes an explicit rational function of the Fibonacci pair \((F_n,F_{n+1})\) alone.  Consequently the limit \(\displaystyle\alpha=\lim_{n\to\infty}R_{2n}\) exists and equals \(\frac32+\frac{\sqrt5}{2}=p+\sqrt q\) with \(p=\frac32,\;q=\frac54\).
